Basically the process:

Make sure the front of all the cells you are going to use have tabs (IOW they have tabbing wire attached to them and it is long enough to solder to the next cell) There are three types of cells you can buy:

Untabbed. For untabbed cells you have to solder a strip of tabbing wire to the strips on the front of each cell. These are the least convenient to work with.

Short tabbed. For short tabbed cells, there is already a strip of tabbing wire on them but it is too short to reach the next cell in the string. It is pretty easy to solder a longer piece of tabbing wire to the end

Fully tabbed. These have full length tabbing wire that will reach the next cell and are the easiest to work with.

For this project, I was using short-tabbed cells.

Lay out your cells face down in strips. You'll have to figure out how you want the layout to be. For this one, I started with 4 strips of 6 for 24 cells. I found the voltage to be insufficient under load and had to add another strip of 4 and if I did it over I would have made 4 strips of 7 instead.

Make it so the tabbing from the front side of the previous cell is lined up with the (2-5 per cell) solder points on the back side of the next cell. This puts the cells in series. Wet the solder points and tabbing wire with a flux pen and solder it.

Shitty paint diagram

The front of the cell is negative and the back is positive. Most people put a strip of duct tape or gorilla tape along the back of the whole strip of cells to add stability and make it easier to handle and give the glue something to stick to. Be aware that once the tape sticks to the cell, you will not be able to remove it it without breaking it.

After you finish building (and testing) your strips of cells, put a strip of glue or epoxy along the strip and stick it down. Put each string of cells next to each other in alternating directions (so they will be in series)

Solder a piece of wire to connect each string together merging the two tabbing wires.
